content: The Blue 88 pill was a blue-colored pharmaceutical compound primarily composed of barbiturates, which are sedative drugs. It was specifically formulated to manage symptoms of battle fatigue, now recognized as combat stress reaction or acute stress disorder, in American soldiers during World War II. Its primary use was to induce sleep and provide temporary relief from the psychological and physical toll of combat. During World War II, the use of this medication was highlighted in a 1994 documentary titled Battle of the Bulge, part of the American Experience series produced by WGBH Educational Foundation in Boston, Massachusetts. This documentary examined the critical German offensive in the Ardennes region of France during the winter of 1944-1945 and provided insights into the medical and psychological challenges faced by Allied forces. As the Allied forces experienced increasing casualties during the Ardennes Offensive, there was a significant shortage of soldiers. Those who were not severely injured or incapacitated by battle fatigue were often encouraged to return to the front lines. Captain Ben Kimmelman, a dental officer with the 4th Medical Battalion Special Troops of the 4th Infantry Division, was actively involved in the medical corps during this period. He observed firsthand the devastating effects of the battle, noting that one in four soldiers wounded during the Battle of the Bulge were classified as psychiatric casualties, a term used to describe those suffering from severe psychological trauma. Captain Kimmelman himself was later captured, along with the rest of the 2-8 Infantry Regiment, also known as Easy Company, during the German campaign. Despite his capture, he survived the war.
